meta.title: Who really said "Music is a moral law. It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Plato. This line appears nowhere in his works — it was first pinned on him in Sir John Lubbock's 1889 book The Pleasures of Life. A documented misattribution.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Music is a moral law. It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Plato. The line surfaces first in Sir John Lubbock's 1889 The Pleasures of Life, credited to Plato with no source. A Victorian-era misattribution.

answer.label: Not Plato — a Victorian-era misattribution
answer.authorName: Falsely credited to Plato; earliest documented in Sir John Lubbock (1889)
answer.authorDates: Plato: c. 428–348 BC · the misquote: first printed 1889
answer.sourceLine: This exact sentiment is not found in any dialogue of Plato. Its earliest documented appearance is Sir John Lubbock’s The Pleasures of Life, Part II (1889, p. 120), which opens its music chapter with the words credited to “Plato” but gives no source — and no such passage exists in the Greek. Wikiquote lists it as Misattributed. The popular wording (“charm and gaiety to life and to everything”) is a later, slightly garbled variant of Lubbock’s already-invented text.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Pleasures of Life, Part II

source.excerpt: Music is a moral law. It gives a soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, a charm to sadness, gaiety and life to everything. It is the essence of order, and leads to all that is good, just, and beautiful, of which it is the invisible, but nevertheless dazzling, passionate, and eternal form.
trail: The exact sentence — “Music is a moral law. It gives a soul to the universe…” — first appears credited to Plato in Sir John Lubbock’s The Pleasures of Life, Part II (1889), with no source given.

Wikiquote lists the line under ‘Misattributed,’ noting it “is not known to exist in Plato’s writings” and “apparently first appeared… in The Pleasures of Life, Part II by Sir John Lubbock… published in 1889.”
The Wikiquote Talk page and researcher Ian Chadwick both trace the misattribution to Lubbock’s 1889 book, p. 120, and find no matching passage in Timaeus or elsewhere in Plato.
source.excerptNote: As printed — credited to “Plato” — at the head of the ‘Music’ chapter in Sir John Lubbock’s The Pleasures of Life, Part II (1889). No corresponding passage exists in Plato. The now-common short form (“charm and gaiety to life and to everything”) is a later paraphrase of these words.

source.rightsNote: The earliest documented source of this text, Sir John Lubbock’s The Pleasures of Life, Part II, was published in 1889 — long before 1931 — so that text is in the public domain in the United States. The short modern wording is an anonymous later paraphrase of that public-domain passage; it too carries no active copyright. (Plato himself, of course, never wrote it.)

author.name: Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury)
author.heading: The Victorian polymath who pinned it on Plato
author.metaLine: 1834–1913 · English banker, biologist, MP & popular essayist
author.bio: Sir John Lubbock, 1st Baron Avebury, was a banker, Liberal MP, archaeologist and naturalist — a friend of Darwin who coined the terms ‘Palaeolithic’ and ‘Neolithic’ and championed the Bank Holidays Act. His hugely popular self-improvement volumes The Pleasures of Life (1887–1889) sprinkled uplifting epigraphs through their chapters. The music chapter of Part II (1889) opens with the “Music is a moral law” passage credited to Plato — the earliest known appearance of the line, with no source cited. Whether Lubbock invented, translated, or copied it from an unknown intermediary is not established, but no such text exists in Plato.

misattribution.heading: A misattribution over a century old
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most-shared ‘Plato’ quotes — on posters, T-shirts and concert programmes — yet it is not in Plato. The trail dead-ends in a Victorian self-help book, not an ancient dialogue.

items.why: No passage matching this line exists in Plato’s dialogues, including Timaeus, the one long known to medieval readers. Wikiquote files it under ‘Misattributed,’ noting it “is not known to exist in Plato’s writings.”

Lubbock’s 1889 text reads “a charm to sadness, gaiety and life to everything.” The now-standard “charm and gaiety to life and to everything” is a smoothed-down later rewrite of that already-invented passage — a misquote of a misattribution, as documented by Ian Chadwick.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest anyone can document this line is 1889, in Sir John Lubbock’s The Pleasures of Life — credited to Plato, but sourced to nothing. Plato never wrote it.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Plato
lead: Plato did take music seriously as a moral force — in the Republic and Laws he argues that musical modes shape character and that a well-ordered soul mirrors musical harmony. That genuine reputation makes the feel-good epigraph plausible enough that few readers question it.

But plausibility is not provenance. A line that sounds like something Plato might have believed still has to be found in what Plato actually wrote — and this one never has been. Its documented life begins in a Victorian essayist’s chapter heading, then snowballs through quotation dictionaries and, later, the internet.
context.pull: A misquote of a misattribution — sourced to nothing older than 1889.
